article: Nautical style's most recognizable element, the Breton-striped shirt, has a precise origin: French naval regulations standardized it for sailors in 1858, specifying the exact number of stripes (21, reportedly for Napoleon's naval victories) to make a man overboard easier to spot against the sea. Coco Chanel adopted the stripe into womenswear in 1917, having encountered it on the Normandy coast, and that single design decision is what fashion historians most consistently credit with launching nautical style's century-long run as a recurring civilian fashion reference, entirely separate from any actual maritime use. Designer Jean Paul Gaultier later made the Breton stripe into something close to a personal signature across decades of his own collections, keeping the look in steady circulation through the late 20th century. The look's most recent revival arrives through 2020s internet-aesthetic tags like sailorcore, which narrow nautical's broad century-spanning reference pool down to a more specific, moodboard-ready coastal mood.
